title: Schema and Item Modeling
readerIntent: Understand how Nodics turns business concepts into governed, provider-independent data contracts.
owner: Owning business modules plus Nodics schema and data-model capabilities
summary: A schema defines a business record once; Nodics builds the corresponding item-model behavior and delegates persistence through configured database contracts.

sections.heading: What is Schema and Item Modeling?
paragraphs: A schema describes the structure and rules of a business record, such as an Employee, Product, Address, or Warehouse. An item model gives application code a governed way to create, read, update, validate, relate, and persist records that follow that schema.
A schema is like a well-designed business form: it defines the fields, relationships, required information, and rules before records are accepted.

sections.heading: Business value
items: Use consistent business definitions across APIs, workflows, imports, search, and BackOffice.
Change supported database providers without moving business ownership into an adapter.
Express relationships, tenant boundaries, access policy, validation, indexing, and versioning intent as governed metadata.
Extend customer-specific fields through layered modules instead of copying the original model.

sections.heading: Schema, item model, and search model
items: The schema is the authoritative structural and behavioral contract owned by a capability.
The item model represents authoritative record operations through the Nodics data framework.
The search model represents query and index behavior for schemas that enable search.
Neither a business service nor a frontend should bypass these contracts to access a database or search engine directly.

sections.heading: What a schema describes
items: Stable business identity, fields, data types, defaults, requirements, and descriptive metadata.
Indexes, uniqueness, relationships, ownership, lifecycle, and versioning choices.
Declarative validation and access metadata applied consistently.
Fields participating in APIs, import, export, display, and search.
Supported extension points for later project modules.

sections.heading: Authority boundaries
paragraphs: The business capability defines its schemas. Nodics data and database capabilities compose runtime models and delegate persistence to the configured provider. A business module does not create a direct database connection or duplicate provider-specific models.

A search model describes searchable behavior but does not replace the item model as source of truth. Clients may render schema metadata, but backend schemas and services remain authoritative for validation and permissions.

sections.heading: Relationships across capabilities
paragraphs: A model can refer to another model owned by the same or a different module. For example, an Enterprise can refer to a Tenant owned by Profile and relate to addresses and contacts.

Each owner validates access and lifecycle. A schema-driven UI may select an existing related record or create a new one only when the target model exposes that operation and the employee has permission.

sections.heading: Versioned and publishable data
paragraphs: Versioning and publishing are configurable per owning module or schema. Content or catalog data may require staged versions and approval before publishing to a separate online system, while a user identity schema may not.
Enabling versioning adds the approved publishing contract; it does not create a parallel staging mechanism.

sections.heading: Example: employee record
paragraphs: An Employee schema identifies the employee and relates it to tenant, enterprise, groups, contacts, and addresses. Friendly display metadata lets BackOffice show code and description rather than only an opaque identifier.

Creation validates required fields, relationship permissions, tenant scope, uniqueness, and business rules. Persistence flows through framework models, search uses the corresponding search contract, and later project modules extend approved metadata without replacing Profile ownership.

sections.heading: Modeling decisions to document
items: Why the model exists and which capability owns it.
How users identify records and which fields are safe for display.
Relationship cardinality, ownership, selection, nested creation, and deletion.
Tenant, enterprise, catalog, site, store, country, channel, or customer scope.
Validation, permissions, states, versioning, publishing, audit, and retention.
Search, cache, import, export, event, and migration implications.
